papers.abstract: Efficiently updating multilingual knowledge in large language models (LLMs), while preserving consistent factual representations across languages, remains a long-standing and unresolved challenge.While deploying separate editing systems for each language might seem viable, this approach incurs substantial costs due to the need to manage multiple models.A more efficient solution involves integrating knowledge updates across all languages into a unified model.However, performing sequential edits across languages often leads to destructive parameter interference, significantly degrading multilingual generalization and the accuracy of injected knowledge.To address this challenge, we propose LangEdit, a novel null-space constrained framework designed to precisely isolate language-specific knowledge updates.The core innovation of LangEdit lies in its ability to project parameter updates for each language onto the orthogonal complement of previous updated subspaces.This approach mathematically guarantees update independence while preserving multilingual generalization capabilities.We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across three model architectures, six languages, and four downstream tasks, demonstrating that LangEdit effectively mitigates parameter interference and outperforms existing state-of-the-art editing methods.Our results highlight its potential for enabling efficient and accurate multilingual knowledge updates in LLMs.The code is available at https: //github.com/VRCMF/LangEdit.git.

papers.title: Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions: Toward Interpretable and Efficient Multilingual Control for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode language identity, and can we identify sparse, consistent dimensions that control the cross-lingual transition from shared representations to language-specific token spaces?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that cross-lingual transfer in LLMs is governed by a sparse, consistent set of language-specific dimensions in the residual stream, and introduces a training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions for controlled language switching.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific dimensions are a consistent and controllable mechanism underlying cross-lingual transfer in LLMs, enabling efficient and interpretable multilingual control through simple, training-free interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific dimensions are sparse and appear at consistent indices across intermediate to final layers of LLMs.
These dimensions can be identified with as few as 50 sentences of parallel or monolingual data.
Intervening on these dimensions by overwriting their values can switch the model's output language while preserving semantic content.
The proposed method outperforms prior neuron-based approaches (Neuron-Kojima and Neuron-Tang) on a multilingual generation control task.
There is significant overlap in language-specific dimensions across typologically similar languages (e.g., Chinese and Japanese share many dimensions).
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters (e.g., anchor layer, scaling coefficient) were primarily tuned on Llama2-7B and transferred to other models (Llama3.1-8B, Aya23-8B), which may be suboptimal.
Evaluation is limited to multilingual generation control and question answering tasks; broader impact on downstream tasks (e.g., mathematics, summarization) and robustness across prompt formulations remains unexamined.
future_direction: Conduct systematic per-model hyperparameter search to optimize performance for each model individually.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of downstream tasks, incorporate task-specific metrics and human judgments, and assess robustness across different prompt formulations.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities despite limited exposure to non-English data. Prior studies show that English-centric large language models map multilingual content into English-aligned representations at intermediate layers and then project them back into target-language token spaces in the final layer. From this observation, we hypothesize that this cross-lingual transition is governed by a small and sparse set of dimensions, which occur at consistent indices across the intermediate to final layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a simple, training-free method to identify and manipulate these dimensions, requiring only as few as 50 sentences of either parallel or monolingual data. Experiments on a multilingual generation control task reveal the interpretability of these dimensions, demonstrating that the interventions in these dimensions can switch the output language while preserving semantic content, and that it surpasses the performance of prior neuron-based approaches at a substantially lower cost.

papers.title: Diagnosing Knowledge Conflict in Multimodal Long-Chain Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in long chain-of-thought reasoning often fail when different knowledge sources provide conflicting signals. We formalize these failures under a unified notion of knowledge conflict, distinguishing input-level objective conflict from process-level effective conflict. Through probing internal representations, we reveal that: (I) Linear Separability: different conflict types are explicitly encoded as linearly separable features rather than entangled; (II) Depth Localization: conflict signals concentrate in mid-to-late layers, indicating a distinct processing stage for conflict encoding; (III) Hierarchical Consistency: aggregating noisy token-level signals along trajectories robustly recovers input-level conflict types; and (IV) Directional Asymmetry: reinforcing the model's implicit source preference under conflict is far easier than enforcing the opposite source. Our findings provide a mechanism-level view of multimodal reasoning under knowledge conflict and enable principled diagnosis and control of long-CoT failures.

papers.title: The Emergence of Abstract Thought in Large Language Models Beyond Any Language
papers.research_question: Do LLMs think in the distinct space of each language, or do they operate in a higher-level language-agnostic space beyond any specific language? Does the trend of non-English performance compared to English indicate the emergence of abstract thought within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs progressively develop a core language-agnostic parameter space (shared neurons) that underlies generalization across languages and supports abstract thought. Based on this, neuron-specific training strategies are proposed to enhance multilingual capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Shared neurons form a compact, language-agnostic set that supports abstract reasoning across languages, and neuron-specific training strategies can enhance multilingual performance.
papers.key_findings:
The proportion of language-shared neurons increases with model evolution and correlates with multilingual ability.
Language-shared neurons become more functionally important than language-exclusive neurons, evolving into language-agnostic neurons that support abstract thought.
Neuron-targeted training based on the language-agnostic score effectively improves multilingual performance, with different strategies for models at different developmental stages.
papers.limitation: Limited by computational resources, restricting evaluation on larger LLMs and full exploration of neuron-centric training at larger scales.
future_direction: Evaluation on larger LLMs and exploration of neuron-centric training at larger scales.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance, their capacity to function effectively across a diverse range of languages has shown marked improvement. Preliminary studies observe that the hidden activations of LLMs often resemble English, even when responding to non-English prompts. This has led to the widespread assumption that LLMs may "think" in English. However, more recent results showing strong multilingual performance, even surpassing English performance on specific tasks in other languages, challenge this view. In this work, we find that LLMs progressively develop a core language-agnostic parameter space-a remarkably small subset of parameters whose deactivation results in significant performance degradation across all languages. This compact yet critical set of parameters underlies the model's ability to generalize beyond individual languages, supporting the emergence of abstract thought that is not tied to any specific linguistic system. Specifically, we identify language-related neurons-those are consistently activated during the processing of particular languages, and categorize them as either shared (active across multiple languages) or exclusive (specific to one). As LLMs undergo continued development over time, we observe a marked increase in both the proportion and functional importance of shared neurons, while exclusive neurons progressively diminish in influence. These shared neurons constitute the backbone of the core language-agnostic parameter space, supporting the emergence of abstract thought. Motivated by these insights, we propose neuron-specific training strategies tailored to LLMs' language-agnostic levels at different development stages. Experiments across diverse LLM families support our approach.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Shapley Head Pruning: Identifying and Removing Interference in Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: How can interference in multilingual transformers be reduced by identifying and pruning language-specific attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Shapley Head Pruning, a method to identify and remove language-specific attention heads in multilingual transformers, reducing interference and improving cross-lingual performance without adding parameters.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Shapley Head Pruning effectively identifies and removes interfering attention heads, improving cross-lingual performance and providing insights into language-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Attention Head Shapley Values exhibit language affinity, with some heads being language-specific and others language-agnostic.
Pruning attention heads with negative Shapley Values improves accuracy on XNLI and UDPOS tasks, with gains up to 24.7%.
Zero-shot pruning using Shapley Values from English can benefit other languages, but not all, indicating transferability.
Language-agnostic attention heads match synonyms across sentences, while language-specific heads have varied behavior.
The method outperforms random pruning and gradient-based baselines in iterative pruning evaluations.
papers.limitation:
Computational cost of Shapley Values is high compared to gradient-based methods.
Reliance on attention visualization for analysis, which may not be a sound analytical tool.
future_direction: Systematically understand relationships between linguistic features, training data volume, and language-specificity of attention heads.
Reduce cross-lingual interference during pre-training, such as pruning during pretraining or utilizing sparsely activated networks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual transformer-based models demonstrate remarkable zero and few-shot transfer across languages by learning and reusing language-agnostic features. However, as a fixed-size model acquires more languages, its performance across all languages degrades, a phenomenon termed interference. Often attributed to limited model capacity, interference is commonly addressed by adding additional parameters despite evidence that transformer-based models are overparameterized. In this work, we show that it is possible to reduce interference by instead identifying and pruning language-specific parameters. First, we use Shapley Values, a credit allocation metric from coalitional game theory, to identify attention heads that introduce interference. Then, we show that removing identified attention heads from a fixed model improves performance for a target language on both sentence classification and structural prediction, seeing gains as large as 24.7\%. Finally, we provide insights on language-agnostic and language-specific attention heads using attention visualization.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning? Are they essential for pattern matching in ICL?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that induction heads are essential for few-shot in-context learning, as their ablation leads to significant performance drops in both abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks.
papers.conclusion: The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, and induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying ICL.
papers.key_findings:
Ablation of 1% of induction heads leads to substantial ICL performance decreases (up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks).
For NLP tasks, ablation of induction heads reduces the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot performance close to zero-shot.
Attention knockout experiments show that blocking the induction pattern causes performance drops comparable to full head ablations, confirming the specific role of the prefix matching and copying mechanism.
The effects are consistent across two models (Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B).
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of prefix matching and copying for pattern matching.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for induction heads without mechanistic verification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks, not verified across NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL).However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking.This paper explores the role of induction heads in a fewshot ICL setting.We analyse two state-of-theart models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks.Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random.For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts.We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present finegrained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer in Multilingual Recurrent Neural Networks.
papers.research_question: Does exposure to a related language (L1) improve implicit syntactic knowledge in a target language (L2) within multilingual neural networks? Do these networks induce a common representation space with shared syntactic categories?
papers.core_contribution: Cross-lingual syntactic transfer in multilingual neural networks is limited and inconsistent, and optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.
papers.conclusion: Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge is limited and dependent on language pairs, and modern multilingual neural networks are still far from acquiring a true interlingua.
papers.key_findings:
Exposing a model to a related language does not always improve grammatical knowledge in the target language; in some cases, it causes negative interference.
Transfer of purely grammatical knowledge (e.g., long-range agreement in nonce sentences) is very limited and strongly dependent on the specific source-target language pair.
Part-of-speech categories are shared to a moderate extent across languages in the models, but dependency categories are not shared at all.
Language relatedness is the most determining factor for both word embedding alignment and part-of-speech transfer.
Scaling from two to nine input languages improves part-of-speech transfer among related languages but worsens it between unrelated languages.
papers.limitation:
Transfer of syntactic knowledge is limited and inconsistent, with negative interference observed in some language pairs (e.g., French to Italian).
Syntactic knowledge transfer within the models is shallow, with dependency categories not shared across languages.
papers.abstract: It is now established that modern neural language models can be successfully trained on multiple languages simultaneously without changes to the underlying architecture. But what kind of knowledge is really shared among languages within these models? Does multilingual training mostly lead to an alignment of the lexical representation spaces or does it also enable the sharing of purely grammatical knowledge? In this paper we dissect different forms of cross-lingual transfer and look for its most determining factors, using a variety of models and probing tasks. We find that exposing our LMs to a related language does not always increase grammatical knowledge in the target language, and that optimal conditions for lexical-semantic transfer may not be optimal for syntactic transfer.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Can you map it to English? The Role of Cross-Lingual Alignment in Multilingual Performance of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on NLU tasks, and does misalignment causally explain failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cross-lingual alignment with English in middle layers is associated with and causally affects LLM performance on multilingual NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual semantic alignment in localized middle layers contributes causally to non-English correctness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Success (TS) instances exhibit higher cross-lingual alignment with English than Transfer Failure (TF) instances.
Activation patching of English activations into non-English forward passes can correct incorrect predictions, indicating causal role of alignment.
Middle layers (e.g., layers 16-25) are critical for alignment and effective patching.
Control patching experiments show that semantic alignment, not just target token bias, drives corrections in specific middle layers.
Alignment peaks in middle layers and varies by language typology, with closer languages to English showing higher alignment.
papers.limitation:
Scope restricted to discriminative NLU tasks.
Benchmarks may have translation artifacts due to human translation from English.
Only analyzes bilingual alignment with English, not between other languages.
future_direction: Exploring targeted steering at inference time to leverage English activations for enhancing performance on non-English languages.
Studying potential downsides such as inflated confidence and erasure of valuable local, non-English knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer prompts in many languages, despite being trained predominantly on English; yet, the mechanisms driving this generalization remain poorly understood. This work asks: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on natural language understanding (NLU) tasks? We study the role of representation alignment in instance-level task decisions, complementing prior analyses conducted both at the language level and task-independently. We introduce the Discriminative Alignment Index ($\DALI$) to quantify instance-level alignment across 24 languages other than English and three distinct NLU tasks. Results show that incorrect NLU predictions are strongly associated with lower representation alignment with English in the model's middle layers. Through activation patching, we show that incorrect predictions in languages other than English can be fixed by patching their parallel English activations in the middle layers, thereby demonstrating the causal role of representation (mis)alignment in cross-lingual correctness.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Linguistic Neuron Overlap Patterns to Facilitate Cross-lingual Transfer on Low-resource Languages
papers.research_question: How can we improve cross-lingual capabilities of LLMs on low-resource languages by selecting an optimal bridge language in Cross-lingual In-Context Learning (X-ICL), and whether sharing neurons can facilitate cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes BridgeX-ICL, a method to improve zero-shot cross-lingual in-context learning for low-resource languages by selecting an optimal bridge language based on neuron overlap patterns and an HSIC-based similarity metric.
papers.conclusion: Explores whether sharing neurons can improve LLMs' cross-lingual performance on low-resource languages and proposes BridgeX-ICL, a language-bridge approach validated on multiple cross-lingual tasks and language pairs.
papers.key_findings:
Strong neural overlaps align with human linguistic taxonomy within language families, but do not consistently hold across families.
Overlapping neurons embody shared semantic information, regardless of the language within or between families.
BridgeX-ICL improves performance on cross-lingual tasks (BLI and MRC) across 15 language pairs by an average of 6.02% and 5.25% over zero-shot baselines.
English is selected as the optimal bridge in 9 out of 15 language pairs in LLaMA (7 out of 15 in Mistral), indicating high-resource, Latin-script languages tend to be the default bridge, but non-Latin script languages like Chinese also show potential.
papers.limitation:
Limited coverage of language pairs and tasks due to lack of comprehensive benchmarks for low-resource languages.
The proposed linguistic distance measurement is probe-data-induced, offering qualitative but not quantitative insights.
Bridge selection reflects training biases of LLMs, inevitably reflecting their training data distribution.
papers.abstract:
The current Large Language Models (LLMs) face significant challenges in improving their
performance on low-resource languages and urgently need data-efficient methods without
costly fine-tuning. From the perspective of language-bridge, we propose a simple yet effective method, namely BridgeXICL,
to improve the zero-shot Cross-lingual In-Context Learning (X-ICL) for low-resource languages. Unlike existing works focusing on
language-specific neurons, BridgeX-ICL explores whether sharing neurons can improve
cross-lingual performance in LLMs. We construct neuron probe data from the groundtruth
MUSE bilingual dictionaries, and define a subset of language overlap neurons accordingly to ensure full activation of these anchored
neurons. Subsequently, we propose
an HSIC-based metric to quantify LLMs’ internal linguistic spectrum based on overlapping neurons, guiding optimal bridge selection.
The experiments conducted on 4 crosslingual tasks and 15 language pairs from 7 diverse families, covering both high-low and moderate-low pairs, validate the effectiveness of BridgeX-ICL and offer empirical insights into the underlying multilingual mechanisms of LLMs. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/
xuyuemei/BridgeX-ICL.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: The Rise and Down of Babel Tower: Investigating the Evolution Process of Multilingual Code Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do the multilingual capabilities of LLMs evolve during the pre-training process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Babel Tower Hypothesis to explain how LLMs evolve multilingual capabilities during pre-training, and introduces a method to optimize pre-training data distribution for multilingual code LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The Babel Tower Hypothesis explains the evolution of multilingual capabilities in LLMs, and optimizing the pre-training data distribution based on this hypothesis significantly improves multilingual performance.
papers.key_findings:
The performance of a new language during pre-training follows three stages: translation (reliance on dominant language), transition, and stabilization (use of own language-specific system).
For some languages, relying on a strong dominant language for translation is more effective than building a new knowledge system with additional data.
The internal state of the LLM, measured via working languages and language-transferring neurons, shifts from the dominant language system to the new language system over training.
Adjusting the pre-training data distribution allows different languages to reach their optimal performance state concurrently.
A method to estimate the optimal pre-training corpus distribution based on training loss and performance leads to models that outperform those trained on the original corpus.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to code languages and smaller models; future work should extend to natural languages and larger models.
future_direction: Extend the approach to natural language scenarios.
Scale to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant multilingual capabilities. However, the mechanisms underlying the development of these capabilities during pre-training are not well understood. In this paper, we use code LLMs as an experimental platform to explore the evolution of multilingual capabilities in LLMs during the pre-training process. Based on our observations, we propose the Babel Tower Hypothesis, which describes the entire process of LLMs acquiring new language capabilities. During the learning process, multiple languages initially share a single knowledge system dominated by the primary language and gradually develop language-specific knowledge systems. We then validate the above hypothesis by tracking the internal states of the LLMs through identifying working languages and language transferring neurons. Experimental results show that the internal state changes of the LLM are consistent with our Babel Tower Hypothesis. Building on these insights, we propose a novel method to construct an optimized pre-training corpus for multilingual code LLMs, which significantly outperforms LLMs trained on the original corpus. The proposed Babel Tower Hypothesis provides new insights into designing pre-training data distributions to achieve optimal multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: One Mind, Many Tongues: A Deep Dive into Language-Agnostic Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons in large language models, considering uncertainty across queries and languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MATRICE, a method for localizing language-agnostic knowledge neurons by quantifying uncertainty across queries and languages, and constructs the RML-LAMA benchmark. It demonstrates these neurons' roles in cross-lingual editing, knowledge enhancement, and injection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed MATRICE method accurately localizes language-agnostic knowledge neurons, and these neurons are shown to be conducive to cross-lingual knowledge editing, enhancement, and injection.
papers.key_findings:
A significant proportion of language-agnostic knowledge neurons are distributed in the last few layers of LLMs.
Manipulating (suppressing/enhancing) language-agnostic knowledge neurons significantly affects knowledge expression across languages.
A single edit on language-agnostic knowledge neurons can simultaneously modify corresponding knowledge in all languages (cross-lingual editing).
Amplifying the activation of language-agnostic knowledge neurons improves prediction performance in low-resource languages.
Fine-tuning only parameters associated with language-agnostic knowledge neurons helps LLMs learn new knowledge while alleviating forgetting of old knowledge.
papers.limitation: The approach is based on knowledge neuron theory and focuses on factual knowledge, not yet extended to other types like commonsense or event knowledge.
future_direction: Extend the approach to investigate other types of knowledge, such as commonsense knowledge and event knowledge.
Adapt the method to new theoretical frameworks as the theory of knowledge neurons evolves.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have learned vast amounts of factual knowledge through self-supervised pre-training on large-scale corpora. Meanwhile, LLMs have also demonstrated excellent multilingual capabilities, which can express the learned knowledge in multiple languages. However, the knowledge storage mechanism in LLMs still remains mysterious. Some researchers attempt to demystify the factual knowledge in LLMs from the perspective of knowledge neurons, and subsequently discover language-agnostic knowledge neurons that store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language barriers. However, the preliminary finding suffers from two limitations: 1) High Uncertainty in Localization Results. Existing study only uses a prompt-based probe to localize knowledge neurons for each fact, while LLMs cannot provide consistent answers for semantically equivalent queries. Thus, it leads to inaccurate localization results with high uncertainty. 2) Lack of Analysis in More Languages. The study only analyzes language-agnostic knowledge neurons on English and Chinese data, without exploring more language families and languages. Naturally, it limits the generalizability of the findings. To address aforementioned problems, we first construct a new benchmark called Rephrased Multilingual LAMA (RML-LAMA), which contains high-quality cloze-style multilingual parallel queries for each fact. Then, we propose a novel method named Multilingual Integrated Gradients with Uncertainty Estimation (MATRICE), which quantifies the uncertainty across queries and languages during knowledge localization. Extensive experiments show that our method can accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons. We also further investigate the role of language-agnostic knowledge neurons in cross-lingual knowledge editing, knowledge enhancement and new knowledge injection.

papers.title: Unveiling Multilinguality in Transformer Models: Exploring Language Specificity in Feed-Forward Networks
papers.research_question: Do neurons in the feed-forward networks of multilingual transformer models exhibit language-specific or language-agnostic behavior across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in multilingual transformer models, feed-forward network layers near the input and output are more language-specific, whereas middle layers are more language-agnostic.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that language specificity in FFNs is higher near the input and output layers, and training data imbalance influences detector activations.
papers.key_findings:
Layers closest to the input and output exhibit more language-specific behavior compared to middle layers.
The number of detectors triggered by English prefixes is higher than for Czech, reflecting training data imbalance.
The number of unique detectors varies across layers, with sparsity patterns observed in FFN activations.
Linear classifiers can predict the language of input prefixes from detector activations with higher accuracy in input and output layers.
Czech-specific detectors decrease in middle layers, suggesting semantic processing uses more language-agnostic detectors.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to only the XGLM model.
Study is centred on the Czech-English language pair, and findings may not generalize to other languages.
Lack of qualitative analysis of linguistic cues triggering detector activation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more language pairs and other multilingual autoregressive language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that the feed-forward module within Transformers can be viewed as a collection of key-value memories, where the keys learn to capture specific patterns from the input based on the training examples. The values then combine the output from the 'memories' of the keys to generate predictions about the next token. This leads to an incremental process of prediction that gradually converges towards the final token choice near the output layers. This interesting perspective raises questions about how multilingual models might leverage this mechanism. Specifically, for autoregressive models trained on two or more languages, do all neurons (across layers) respond equally to all languages? No! Our hypothesis centers around the notion that during pretraining, certain model parameters learn strong language-specific features, while others learn more language-agnostic (shared across languages) features. To validate this, we conduct experiments utilizing parallel corpora of two languages that the model was initially pretrained on. Our findings reveal that the layers closest to the network's input or output tend to exhibit more language-specific behaviour compared to the layers in the middle.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models, and what are the properties of the neurons that store such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization in multilingual PLMs, and discovers two new types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons.
papers.conclusion: The AMIG method effectively localizes knowledge neurons in multilingual PLMs, and the discoveries of language-independent and degenerate knowledge neurons shed light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed AMIG method localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than baseline methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons exist, are concentrated in the final layers, and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist, exhibit functional overlap, and can be used to help PLMs detect wrong facts in a fact-checking task.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models (BERT and GPT-2).
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration on knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: CRANE: Causal Relevance Analysis of Language-Specific Neurons in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are language capabilities organized at the neuron level in multilingual LLMs? The paper redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity and proposes a method to identify language-specific neurons.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CRANE, a relevance-based framework for identifying language-specific neurons by functional necessity, and finds asymmetric, language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations in multilingual LLMs.
papers.conclusion: CRANE provides a framework for studying language-specific neurons based on functional necessity, revealing that language-specific neurons are language-selective but non-exclusive, and highlighting the importance of distinguishing statistical correlation from functional contribution.
papers.key_findings:
CRANE induces targeted functional degradation on the intended language while preserving performance on non-target languages, outperforming activation-based methods like LAPE.
Neuron-level interventions reveal an asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations.
Normalized kurtosis of relevance distributions reveals language-related structure in neuron contributions.
Neuron sets identified on the Base model retain functional influence when transferred to the Chat model, indicating partial preservation of language-specific neurons after instruction tuning.
The proposed LangSpec-F1 metric quantifies language-selective functional effects under neuron intervention.
papers.limitation:
CRANE currently relies on normalized kurtosis to characterize concentration patterns in language-conditioned relevance distributions, which is only one possible statistic.
Functional validation is performed via neuron masking, a relatively coarse intervention; more fine-grained causal techniques may provide deeper insight.
Experiments focus on three languages and a single model family, and open-ended generation evaluation uses an LLM-as-a-judge protocol which may introduce variance.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to broader language coverage, additional architectures, and alternative evaluation paradigms.
Using more fine-grained causal techniques, such as neuron re-weighting or path-specific analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across languages, yet how language capabilities are organized at the neuron level remains poorly understood. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. Prior work has identified language-related neurons mainly through activation-based heuristics, which conflate language preference with functional importance. We propose CRANE, a relevance-based analysis framework that redefines language specificity in terms of functional necessity, identifying language-specific neurons through targeted neuron-level interventions. CRANE characterizes neuron specialization by their contribution to language-conditioned predictions rather than activation magnitude. Our implementation will be made publicly available. Neuron-level interventions reveal a consistent asymmetric pattern: masking neurons relevant to a target language selectively degrades performance on that language while preserving performance on other languages to a substantial extent, indicating language-selective but non-exclusive neuron specializations. Experiments on English, Chinese, and Vietnamese across multiple benchmarks, together with a dedicated relevance-based metric and base-to-chat model transfer analysis, show that CRANE isolates language-specific components more precisely than activation-based methods.

papers.title: How Programming Concepts and Neurons Are Shared in Code Language Models
papers.research_question: How do code language models represent multiple programming languages and English in their concept space? Specifically, do they use a pivot language, and can we identify language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates how code language models represent programming languages and English, finding that English and certain PLs (like C#) are central in the concept space, and that language-specific neurons exist but are challenging to identify for highly aligned PLs.
papers.conclusion: Our findings deepen our understanding of LLMs’ inner workings in the context of PLs and provide valuable insights for interpretability in code-related tasks.
papers.key_findings:
English and PL keywords appear in intermediate layers with high probabilities in the second half of the layers.
C# is highly aligned with other PLs in the model's concept space.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in bottom layers, while PL-exclusive neurons are in top layers.
For highly aligned PLs (like C# and Java), identifying language-specific neurons is challenging.
The model's concept space is closer to English and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in intermediate layers during translation tasks.
papers.limitation:
The super-parallel dataset is limited to seven languages due to source constraints.
Using keywords to interpret latent embeddings may not be precise because some PL keywords lack direct English meanings or map to multiple tokens.
The analysis is limited to Llama-based architectures; exploring other architectures is needed for broader validation.
papers.abstract: Several studies have explored the mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) in coding tasks, but most have focused on programming languages (PLs) in a monolingual setting. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between multiple PLs and English in the concept space of LLMs. We perform a few-shot translation task on 21 PL pairs using two Llama-based models. By decoding the embeddings of intermediate layers during this task, we observe that the concept space is closer to English (including PL keywords) and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in the second half of the intermediate layers. We analyze neuron activations for 11 PLs and English, finding that while language-specific neurons are primarily concentrated in the bottom layers, those exclusive to each PL tend to appear in the top layers. For PLs that are highly aligned with multiple other PLs, identifying language-specific neurons is not feasible. These PLs also tend to have a larger keyword set than other PLs and are closer to the model's concept space regardless of the input/output PL in the translation task. Our findings provide insights into how LLMs internally represent PLs, revealing structural patterns in the model's concept space. Code is available at https://github.com/cisnlp/code-specific-neurons.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Unlocking Multilingual Reasoning Capability of LLMs and LVLMs through Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How to enhance multilingual reasoning capabilities of LLMs and LVLMs without additional training or external tools?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MRRE, a training-free inference-time method that enhances multilingual reasoning in LLMs and LVLMs by steering hidden states with precomputed vectors.
papers.conclusion: Proposes MRRE, a training-free inference-time method that enhances multilingual reasoning in LLMs and LVLMs, with comprehensive results demonstrating effectiveness and generalizability.
papers.key_findings:
MRRE improves non-English reasoning by an average of 5.48% and up to 7.54% in low-resource languages.
MRRE improves input-output language consistency by 3.78%.
MRRE is effective across both LLMs and LVLMs and across different benchmarks.
The method works by aligning non-English hidden states to English in middle layers and then restoring target language in later layers.
The vectors can be generalized across modalities (from LLM to LVLM).
papers.limitation:
MRRE requires access to internal representations, making it infeasible for closed-source models.
Experiments are limited to widely used benchmarks and models due to cost and resource constraints.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning capabilities, yet their performance in English significantly outperforms that in low-resource languages, raising fairness concerns in multilingual applications. Existing approaches either rely on costly multilingual training or employ prompting with external translation tools, both of which are resource-intensive and sensitive to translation quality. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free inference-time method to enhance Multilingual Reasoning capabilities via Representation Engineering (MRRE) without using any additional training data or tools. MRRE sequentially injects two precomputed vectors at specific layers during inference processing: cross-lingual reasoning enhancement vectors, which steer non-English reasoning representations toward English space to unlock multilingual reasoning, and target-language output anchoring vectors, which restore the distribution of the target language to preserve input-output language consistency. Comprehensive experiments across six advanced LLMs and LVLMs on four reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MRRE consistently enhances non-English reasoning by an average gain of 5.48% and up to 7.54% in low-resource languages (Thai and Swahili), while improving input-output language consistency by 3.78%.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Encoders Learn Cross-lingual Representation?
papers.research_question: How do multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations without explicit cross-lingual signals, and what factors influence this process?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation provides a comprehensive analysis of how multilingual encoders like mBERT learn cross-lingual representations, identifying key factors such as parameter sharing, anchor points, and language similarity, and proposes methods like contrastive alignment to improve cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: The thesis concludes that multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations through shared parameters and anchor points, but performance is uneven across languages, and explicit alignment can help. Future work includes scaling to more languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual BERT (mBERT) learns cross-lingual representations without any explicit cross-lingual signal, achieving strong zero-shot transfer across a variety of tasks.
Parameter sharing and anchor points (shared subwords across languages) are crucial for the emergence of cross-lingual representations in multilingual encoders.
Not all languages are equally represented in mBERT; low-resource languages suffer from poor performance due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
Explicit alignment methods, such as contrastive alignment using bitext, can improve cross-lingual representations, but their effectiveness varies across models and language pairs.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer exhibits high variance due to underspecified optimization, and data projection with self-training can constrain and improve transfer performance.
papers.limitation: mBERT performs poorly on low-resource languages due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
future_direction: Continue scaling multilingual encoders to more languages and larger models
Extend to multimodal multilingual models
Improve cross-lingual transfer for low-resource languages
papers.abstract: NLP systems typically require support for more than one language. As different languages have different amounts of supervision, cross-lingual transfer benefits languages with little to no training data by transferring from other languages. From an engineering perspective, multilingual NLP benefits development and maintenance by serving multiple languages with a single system. Both cross-lingual transfer and multilingual NLP rely on cross-lingual representations serving as the foundation. As BERT revolutionized representation learning and NLP, it also revolutionized cross-lingual representations and cross-lingual transfer. Multilingual BERT was released as a replacement for single-language BERT, trained with Wikipedia data in 104 languages. Surprisingly, without any explicit cross-lingual signal, multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual representations in addition to representations for individual languages. This thesis first shows such surprising cross-lingual effectiveness compared against prior art on various tasks. Naturally, it raises a set of questions, most notably how do these multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations. In exploring these questions, this thesis will analyze the behavior of multilingual models in a variety of settings on high and low resource languages. We also look at how to inject different cross-lingual signals into multilingual encoders, and the optimization behavior of cross-lingual transfer with these models. Together, they provide a better understanding of multilingual encoders on cross-lingual transfer. Our findings will lead us to suggested improvements to multilingual encoders and cross-lingual transfer.

papers.title: Counting Hypothesis: Potential Mechanism of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do large language models support in-context learning? What is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the counting hypothesis, which suggests that LLMs support in-context learning by using context-dependent subspaces to encode potential answers and counting the strengths of contexts across examples.
papers.conclusion: The counting hypothesis offers a plausible explanation for ICL, where LLMs use context-dependent subspaces to encode answers and count contextual strengths across examples, supported by component analysis of residual streams.
papers.key_findings:
Residual streams of separator and answer tokens share common components, as shown by dictionary learning and ICA.
The last separator's residual stream aligns with answer token components, especially in deeper layers.
The coding coefficients of the last separator correlate with the minimum distance between answer and separator components.
The ratio R (based on coding coefficients of top components) differs significantly between correct and incorrect predictions, suggesting embedding components are associated with decision-making.
The counting hypothesis is supported by component analysis of residual streams.
papers.limitation:
The ideal case assumptions (e.g., invariance of example order) may not always hold in practice.
The component analysis methods (dictionary learning and ICA) may not be optimal for extracting the subspaces used by LLMs.
future_direction: Explore effective algorithms to investigate LLMs’ subspace associated with decision-making.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) indicates that large language models (LLMs) pretrained on a massive amount of data can learn specific tasks from input prompts' examples. ICL is notable for two reasons. First, it does not need modification of LLMs' internal structure. Second, it enables LLMs to perform a wide range of tasks/functions with a few examples demonstrating a desirable task. ICL opens up new ways to utilize LLMs in more domains, but its underlying mechanisms still remain poorly understood, making error correction and diagnosis extremely challenging. Thus, it is imperative that we better understand the limitations of ICL and how exactly LLMs support ICL. Inspired by ICL properties and LLMs' functional modules, we propose 1the counting hypothesis' of ICL, which suggests that LLMs' encoding strategy may underlie ICL, and provide supporting evidence.

papers.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Why does in-context learning (ICL) emerge and then disappear (transience) during training, and what are the dynamics between ICL and other learning strategies?
papers.core_contribution: The transience of in-context learning (ICL) is explained by coopetition (cooperative and competitive dynamics) between ICL and a newly identified strategy called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), where shared sub-circuits enable ICL emergence before CIWL asymptotically dominates.
papers.conclusion: Strategy coopetition between ICL and CIWL explains the emergence and transience of ICL, providing a deeper mechanistic understanding of how capabilities dynamically trade off during transformer training.
papers.key_findings:
The asymptotic strategy after ICL transience is a hybrid called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), which depends on both in-weights information and the presence of the correct label in context.
ICL and CIWL share critical sub-circuits (e.g., Layer 2 induction heads), leading to cooperative dynamics that enable ICL emergence.
ICL emergence is only possible when CIWL is not fully formed, and ICL is faster to emerge but asymptotically dominated by CIWL.
A minimal mathematical model captures the coopetition dynamics and explains transience.
Matching context and query exemplars in the data can make ICL persistent by removing the asymptotic bias towards CIWL.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a powerful ability that emerges in transformer models, enabling them to learn from context without weight updates. Recent work has established emergent ICL as a transient phenomenon that can sometimes disappear after long training times. In this work, we sought a mechanistic understanding of these transient dynamics. Firstly, we find that, after the disappearance of ICL, the asymptotic strategy is a remarkable hybrid between in-weights and in-context learning, which we term "context-constrained in-weights learning" (CIWL). CIWL is in competition with ICL, and eventually replaces it as the dominant strategy of the model (thus leading to ICL transience). However, we also find that the two competing strategies actually share sub-circuits, which gives rise to cooperative dynamics as well. For example, in our setup, ICL is unable to emerge quickly on its own, and can only be enabled through the simultaneous slow development of asymptotic CIWL. CIWL thus both cooperates and competes with ICL, a phenomenon we term "strategy coopetition." We propose a minimal mathematical model that reproduces these key dynamics and interactions. Informed by this model, we were able to identify a setup where ICL is truly emergent and persistent.

papers.title: The Hidden Space of Safety: Understanding Preference-Tuned LLMs in Multilingual context
papers.research_question: How does alignment (preference tuning) affect the hidden representations of LLMs across different languages, and does it generalize effectively beyond English?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that alignment induces a separation between safe and unsafe representations in the hidden space for English, but this effect is significantly weaker for other languages, highlighting a monolingual bias in current preference-tuning methods.
papers.conclusion: State-of-the-art preference-tuned models exhibit a monolingual bias, with alignment being effective in English but inconsistent across other languages, underscoring the need for language-specific fine-tuning to ensure robust multilingual safety.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment improves cluster separation between harmful and harmless prompts in English but shows inconsistent and weaker effects in Hindi, Chinese, and German.
Quantitative metrics (Bhattacharyya Distance, Silhouette Score) confirm stronger alignment-induced separation in English compared to other languages.
In a parallel text-detoxification setting, alignment fails to induce a clear distribution shift for Hindi, indicating language-dependent representation learning.
The study finds that some models (e.g., for Hindi) can show greater cluster separation in the unaligned reference model than in the aligned model, indicating potential alignment degradation.
Current alignment strategies, optimized on English-centric preference data, do not generalize robustly to multilingual settings, leading to safety inconsistencies.
papers.limitation:
The study primarily focuses on safety alignment, overlooking other critical domains such as multi-modality, reasoning, instruction-following, or planning due to the lack of standardized multilingual benchmarks for these tasks.
Only three non-English languages (Hindi, Chinese, German), all medium-resource, are evaluated, limiting generalizability to low-resource languages.
The dataset consists of 5,000 sentences, which may not fully capture the diversity of real-world multilingual scenarios.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to low-resource languages to better understand alignment disparities.
Use a broader dataset to further validate findings across different linguistic and cultural contexts.
Prioritize multilingual preference collection and explore synthetic techniques to transfer alignment knowledge from English to other languages.
papers.abstract: Alignment tuning has enabled large language models to excel in reasoning, instruction-following, and minimizing harmful generations. However, despite their widespread deployment, these models exhibit a monolingual bias, raising concerns about the effectiveness of alignment across languages. Current alignment methods predominantly focus on English, leaving it unclear how alignment mechanism generalize to multilingual settings. To address this, we conduct a systematic analysis of distributional shifts in the embedding space of LLMs before and after alignment, uncovering its impact on model behavior across diverse languages. We leverage the alignment-induced separation in safety space as a quantitative tool to measure how alignment enforces safety constraints.
