Our study evaluates seven LLMs using balanced toxicity datasets and parallel text-detoxification benchmarks, revealing substantial disparities in the latent representation space between high-resource and low-resource languages. These findings underscore the need for language-specific fine-tuning to ensure fair, reliable and robust multilingual alignment. Our insights provide a foundation for developing truly safe multilingual LLMs, emphasizing the urgency of addressing alignment gaps in underrepresented languages.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: How do language models internally handle and recall temporally changing facts? Specifically, where within the model architecture does the mechanism for time-specific knowledge reside?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that mediate the recall of time-specific knowledge in LLMs. Ablating these heads degrades temporal fact recall while leaving time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance unaffected, and their activations can be used for temporal knowledge editing.
papers.conclusion: The work systematically uncovers Temporal Heads that selectively mediate time-variant knowledge in LLMs. These heads are causally important for temporal recall, can be activated by both numeric and textual time references, and offer a target for precise temporal knowledge editing without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specific attention heads (Temporal Heads) are identified across multiple models (e.g., a15.h0, a18.h3 in Llama2) that are crucial for recalling time-specific facts.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal impact on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated not only by numeric time conditions (e.g., 'In 2004') but also by textual aliases (e.g., 'In the year the Summer Olympics were held in Athens'), indicating they encode a broader temporal dimension.
The importance of Temporal Heads varies across different years and knowledge categories, with stronger effects around periods of factual transition.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by selectively adjusting the activation values of these heads, demonstrating their role as a key component for modifying time-sensitive information.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs like General ChroKnowledge was constrained, as the underlying multiple-choice options typically do not exhibit temporal dependencies.
The circuit analysis method (EAP-IG) did not support models with Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), excluding models like Llama-3-8B-Instruct from the main analysis.
future_direction: Future work should include broader application of the findings for enhancing temporal reasoning to increase practical value.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how multilingual language models acquire and represent factual knowledge across languages, specifically examining the factors affecting probing performance, whether fact representations are shared or independent across languages, and how cross-lingual representations are formed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes methods for distinguishing three types of fact representations in multilingual language models (language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred) and reveals the challenges in cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: Our research establishes the groundwork for further studies in understanding cross-lingual factual knowledge representation and highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in ML-LMs.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance across languages shows moderate correlation with training data volume and strong negative correlation with mask token count.
There are localized knowledge sharing patterns among geographically proximate languages.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations, even for the same fact.
Active fact neurons in low-resource languages are more active and distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
Cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge does occur but is limited, and many correctly predicted facts in low-resource languages can be attributed to simple inference patterns rather than true transfer.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R) and may not generalize to large decoder-based multilingual models.
future_direction: Enhance the cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs).In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge.Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT).We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts.We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: languageindependent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them.Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs. 1

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Exploring Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation: Mutual Opportunities and Open Challenges
papers.research_question: Can LLMs leverage both their robust capabilities (in English) and their multilingual knowledge (in non-English languages) during inference to further unlock their multilingual potential?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation (X Transplant), a probing framework that transplants latent activations across languages at inference time to unlock multilingual and cultural knowledge in LLMs, revealing underutilized potential.
papers.conclusion: The analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
X Transplant has mutually beneficial effects on multilingual capability and cultural adaptability, especially for low-resource languages and cultures.
Attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge.
The upper-bound performance of X Transplant reveals a significant underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential.
English boosts multilingual capability, while non-English improves cultural adaptability.
papers.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) often exhibit imbalances in multilingual capabilities and cultural adaptability, largely attributed to their English-centric pre-training data. In this paper, we introduce and investigate a cross-lingual latent transplantation (XTransplant) framework, which aims to further exploit the model's internalized multilingual knowledge during inference and examine its effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs. XTransplant framework enables models to harness the complementary strengths of both English and non-English resources by transplanting latent activations across languages. Through extensive analysis, we empirically demonstrate that XTransplant, a form of cross-lingual interaction, has mutually beneficial effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs, particularly for low-resource languages and cultures. We further reveal that attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge. In addition, we conduct in-depth analysis of XTransplant's stability, effectiveness, and generalizability. By probing the upper bound performance of XTransplant, we expose the considerable underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential-a challenge that remains open. We hope our analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Disentangling Language and Culture for Evaluating Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to evaluate multilingual large language models by disentangling linguistic medium and cultural context, and explores the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon where models perform better when questions are culturally aligned with the language.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Dual Evaluation Framework that disentangles language and culture to evaluate multilingual LLMs, and discovers the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon where models perform better when questions are culturally aligned with the language.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal the Cultural-Linguistic Synergy phenomenon, challenging the assumption that LLMs perform uniformly across languages, and highlight the necessity of culturally and linguistically aware model evaluations.
papers.key_findings:
Models perform best on English-speaking culture questions, even when asked in other languages.
Models exhibit Cultural-Linguistic Synergy: better performance when questions are posed in the language corresponding to the cultural context.
A higher proportion of language-specialized neurons are activated when the cultural context aligns with the language, explaining the synergy.
The proportion of specialized neurons can be used as an indicator for comparing multilingual capabilities during training.
The number of activated neurons is strongly correlated with model performance in the corresponding language.
papers.limitation:
The framework requires dual-format question content for robust cross-cultural comparisons, which may not always be available.
The study focuses on a single cultural context per language, not capturing the diversity within languages spoken in multiple regions.
Interpretability probing is limited to smaller models (e.g., 7B and 8B parameters) due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Expand the framework to incorporate more varied cultural contexts for each language.
Extend interpretability analysis to larger models with more parameters.
Further expand the framework for more comprehensive evaluations of multilingual models.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a Dual Evaluation Framework to comprehensively assess the multilingual capabilities of LLMs. By decomposing the evaluation along the dimensions of linguistic medium and cultural context, this framework enables a nuanced analysis of LLMs' ability to process questions within both native and cross-cultural contexts cross-lingually. Extensive evaluations are conducted on a wide range of models, revealing a notable "CulturalLinguistic Synergy" phenomenon, where models exhibit better performance when questions are culturally aligned with the language. This phenomenon is further explored through interpretability probing, which shows that a higher proportion of specific neurons are activated in a language's cultural context. This activation proportion could serve as a potential indicator for evaluating multilingual performance during model training. Our findings challenge the prevailing notion that LLMs, primarily trained on English data, perform uniformly across languages and highlight the necessity of culturally and linguistically model evaluations. Our code can be found at https://yingjiahao14. github.io/Dual-Evaluation/.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Probing Cross-Lingual Lexical Knowledge from Multilingual Sentence Encoders
papers.research_question: How to best leverage multilingual sentence encoders to represent sub-sentence lexical items (words and phrases) in cross-lingual lexical tasks, and how much cross-lingual lexical knowledge is stored in their parameters.
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders can be 'rewired' into effective cross-lingual lexical encoders via an inexpensive contrastive learning procedure requiring only a small dictionary, exposing more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than is available when using them off-the-shelf.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that multilingual sentence encoders can be effectively transformed into cross-lingual lexical encoders via contrastive fine-tuning, exposing rich lexical knowledge that is particularly beneficial for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual sentence encoders (LaBSE, XMPNET) store more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than vanilla multilingual language models (mBERT, XLM-R).
Contrastive cross-lingual lexical fine-tuning with a small dictionary (1k-5k pairs) substantially improves performance on lexical tasks like BLI, XLSIM, and XEL.
Interpolating the fine-tuned encoder representations with static cross-lingual word embeddings (CLWEs) yields further performance gains, especially for low-resource language pairs.
The gains from contrastive fine-tuning are particularly large for low-resource language pairs, indicating the stored lexical knowledge is crucial in data-scarce scenarios.
Multilingual sentence encoders are more resilient to training data scarcity than static CLWE methods like VECMAP.
papers.abstract: Pretrained multilingual language models (LMs) can be successfully transformed into multilingual sentence encoders (SEs; e.g., LaBSE, xMPNet) via additional fine-tuning or model distillation with parallel data. However, it remains unclear how to best leverage them to represent sub-sentence lexical items (i.e., words and phrases) in cross-lingual lexical tasks. In this work, we probe SEs for the amount of cross-lingual lexical knowledge stored in their parameters, and compare them against the original multilingual LMs. We also devise a simple yet efficient method for exposing the cross-lingual lexical knowledge by means of additional fine-tuning through inexpensive contrastive learning that requires only a small amount of word translation pairs. Using bilingual lexical induction (BLI), cross-lingual lexical semantic similarity, and cross-lingual entity linking as lexical probing tasks, we report substantial gains on standard benchmarks (e.g., +10 Precision@1 points in BLI). The results indicate that the SEs such as LaBSE can be 'rewired' into effective cross-lingual lexical encoders via the contrastive learning procedure, and that they contain more cross-lingual lexical knowledge than what 'meets the eye' when they are used as off-the-shelf SEs. This way, we also provide an effective tool for harnessing 'covert' multilingual lexical knowledge hidden in multilingual sentence encoders.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual: Tracing Internal Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do bilingual language models develop internal representations, specifically when, where, and how does bilingual alignment emerge during pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: Bilingual language models first learn languages separately and then gradually form bilingual alignments, particularly in mid-layers, with larger models showing stronger alignment; bilingual representations are critical for performance, as shown by an intervention method that injects bilingual features from a fully trained model into a mid-training model.
papers.conclusion: Bilingual language models initially learn languages independently and later develop bilingual alignments, especially in mid-layers of larger models, and sparse autoencoders can be used for both analysis and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs initially learn languages independently and gradually develop bilingual alignment over training.
Bilingual alignments are more prominently captured in the mid-layers of the model.
Larger models exhibit stronger bilingual alignment than smaller ones.
Bilingual representations from a fully trained model enhance the performance of a mid-training model when injected.
The model's internal representations evolve from language-specific to bilingual semantic alignment as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on English and Japanese, so findings may not generalize to all language pairs.
The interpretability of sparse autoencoders is limited and reconstruction accuracy is not perfect, so analysis is based on an approximation.
future_direction: Investigate a wider range of language pairs to validate and extend the observations.
Combine sparse autoencoders with other analytical methods for a more robust understanding.
papers.abstract: This study explores how bilingual language models develop complex internal representations. We employ sparse autoencoders to analyze internal representations of bilingual language models with a focus on the effects of training steps, layers, and model sizes. Our analysis shows that language models first learn languages separately, and then gradually form bilingual alignments, particularly in the mid layers. We also found that this bilingual tendency is stronger in larger models. Building on these findings, we demonstrate the critical role of bilingual representations in model performance by employing a novel method that integrates decomposed representations from a fully trained model into a mid-training model. Our results provide insights into how language models acquire bilingual capabilities.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Do Multilingual Neural Machine Translation Models Contain Language Pair Specific Attention Heads?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual neural machine translation models contain language pair specific attention heads? The paper investigates this by analyzing individual attention heads in a many-to-one NMT model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in a multilingual NMT model, the most important attention heads are largely language-independent, and about 30% of heads can be pruned without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Although rare language-pair specific attention heads exist, the most important heads are language-independent, and around 30% of heads can be pruned without retraining and with almost no loss in BLEU.
papers.key_findings:
The set of most important attention heads is very similar across different language pairs.
It is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important attention heads without greatly hurting translation quality.
For encoder-decoder (cross) attention heads, the coverage metric is a better indicator for pruning importance, while for encoder self-attention heads, the confidence metric is more effective.
Some rare attention heads are language-pair specific, as identified by the exhaustive Sequential Backward Selection (SBS) procedure.
The variance, confidence, and coverage metrics provide a proxy for head importance, but the SBS algorithm yields the best ranking for pruning.
future_direction: Perform pruning at different levels of granularity (beyond single scalar metrics) to identify which parts of the model are more language-specific.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on the analysis of the multilingual representations focus on identifying whether there is an emergence of languageindependent representations, or whether a multilingual model partitions its weights among different languages. While most of such work has been conducted in a "black-box" manner, this paper aims to analyze individual components of a multilingual neural translation (NMT) model. In particular, we look at the encoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention heads (in a many-to-one NMT model) that are more specific to the translation of a certain language pair than others by (1) employing metrics that quantify some aspects of the attention weights such as "variance" or "confidence", and (2) systematically ranking the importance of attention heads with respect to translation quality. Experimental results show that surprisingly, the set of most important attention heads are very similar across the language pairs and that it is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important heads without hurting the translation quality greatly.

papers.title: Understanding and Controlling Repetition Neurons and Induction Heads in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between repetition neurons and induction heads in in-context learning, and how does their ablation affect ICL performance and repetitive generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a layer-wise analysis showing that repetition neurons in late layers are critical for ICL, while middle-layer neurons can be ablated to reduce repetition without harming ICL, and proposes a three-segment ablation strategy for this purpose.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that repetition neurons and induction heads form a cascade for pattern recognition in ICL, and that selective ablation of middle-layer repetition neurons can reduce repetitive generation while preserving ICL performance.
papers.key_findings:
The impact of repetition neuron ablation on ICL performance varies significantly with layer depth.
Repetition neurons in output-side layers serve as critical executors of pattern-based predictions, with effects on ICL performance comparable to induction heads.
Joint ablation of both repetition neurons and induction heads leads to a near-complete breakdown of pattern recognition.
Selectively deactivating repetition neurons in middle layers reduces repetition while preserving ICL performance.
future_direction: Generalizing the three-step pipeline (behavioral pattern detection, neuron/head ranking, targeted ablation) to other problems like memorization.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize repetitive input patterns and their performance on in-context learning (ICL). In contrast to prior work that has primarily focused on attention heads, we examine this relationship from the perspective of skill neurons, specifically repetition neurons. Our experiments reveal that the impact of these neurons on ICL performance varies depending on the depth of the layer in which they reside. By comparing the effects of repetition neurons and induction heads, we further identify strategies for reducing repetitive outputs while maintaining strong ICL capabilities.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Extracting Interpretable Task-Specific Circuits from Large Language Models for Faster Inference
papers.research_question: Is it possible to extract the minimal subset from an LLM that is able to perform a specific task in a faster, standalone manner?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel method to automatically extract task-specific circuits from large language models without additional training, resulting in smaller, faster, and more interpretable submodels.
papers.conclusion: The method successfully extracts task-specific circuits from LLMs, enabling standalone usage with reduced size and inference time, and aligns with prior circuit identification results.
papers.key_findings:
The pruned models achieve up to 82.77% reduction in parameters while maintaining or improving task accuracy.
Mean ablation yields smaller models than zero ablation with better performance consistency.
The extracted circuits include most important components identified in previous manual circuit analyses.
Pruning irrelevant attention heads is prioritized over MLPs in the extraction process.
The method outperforms knowledge distillation with small data samples.
future_direction: Metric selection for different tasks
Study of phenomena like accuracy-KL divergence correlation in greater-than task
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks. However, the size of LLMs is steadily increasing, hindering their application on computationally constrained environments. On the other hand, despite their general capabilities, there are many situations where only one specific task is performed, rendering all other capabilities unnecessary and wasteful. This leads us to the following question: Is it possible to extract the minimal subset from an LLM that is able to perform a specific task in a faster, standalone manner? Recent works on Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) have shown that specific tasks are performed by a localized subset of components, or circuit. However, current techniques used to identify the circuit cannot be used to extract it for its standalone usage. In this work, we propose a novel approach to automatically extract the subset of the LLM that properly performs a targeted task requiring no additional training and a small amount of data samples. We evaluate our approach on different tasks and show that the resulting models are (i) considerably smaller, reducing the number of parameters up to 82.77% and (ii) more interpretable, as they focus on the circuit that is used to carry out the specific task, and can therefore be understood using MI techniques.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can inference-time neuron activation steering improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models without additional training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time method that modulates neuron activations to improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by rebalancing shared and language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: CLAS effectively improves cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by steering activations to promote functional divergence, with gains not reliant on geometric alignment to the anchor language.
papers.key_findings:
CLAS achieves average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) on classification and generation benchmarks, respectively.
Performance improvements are driven by functional divergence, with gains correlating with increased language cluster separation rather than closer alignment to English.
CLAS reduces cosine similarity to English for non-anchor languages, indicating a shift away from strict geometric alignment.
Qualitative analysis shows CLAS suppresses repetition loops and verbosity in generation outputs.
The steering parameter alpha can be positive or negative for optimal performance, indicating task- and model-dependent balance between shared and language-specific signals.
papers.limitation:
Analysis and intervention are anchored to English, which may not generalize to other anchor languages.
CLAS is not uniformly beneficial and can cause performance regressions for some languages.
Mechanistic analysis does not isolate attention heads or other circuit components, limiting causal attribution.
future_direction: Explore adaptive steering strategies based on representational structure.
Better understand saturation effects in well-separated language clusters.
Extend CLAS to other modalities and training settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on classification and generation benchmarks, achieving average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) respectively, while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment; performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

papers.title: A Shared Geometry of Difficulty in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether problem-difficulty representations in multilingual LLMs are language-specific or shared across languages, and how they are encoded depth-dependently.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode problem difficulty in a depth-dependent manner: early layers form a language-agnostic representation that supports cross-lingual transfer, while deeper layers refine it into language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form a language-agnostic estimate of difficulty in early layers before specializing it to individual languages in deeper layers, indicating a shared geometry of difficulty across languages.
papers.key_findings:
Difficulty is linearly decodable from both shallow (early) and deep (later) transformer layers.
Probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages than those trained on deep representations.
Probes trained on deep representations achieve higher accuracy within the same language but generalize poorly across languages.
There is a trade-off between cross-lingual generalization and language-specific accuracy, with optimal layers differing for same-language vs. cross-lingual evaluation.
This depth-dependent organization of difficulty representations is consistent across multiple LLM architectures and scales.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is confined to mathematical problem solving using the AMC subset of Easy2Hard, so it is unclear if findings extend to other domains.
Empirical evaluation is limited to a small set of instruction-tuned, decoder-only language models.
Conclusions are based exclusively on probing analyses without causal evidence for the role of difficulty signals in inference.
future_direction: Whether difficulty-based interventions learned in one language transfer to other languages.
papers.abstract: Predicting problem-difficulty in large language models (LLMs) refers to estimating how difficult a task is according to the model itself, typically by training linear probes on its internal representations. In this work, we study the multilingual geometry of problem-difficulty in LLMs by training linear probes using the AMC subset of the Easy2Hard benchmark, translated into 21 languages. We found that difficulty-related signals emerge at two distinct stages of the model internals, corresponding to shallow (early-layers) and deep (later-layers) internal representations, that exhibit functionally different behaviors. Probes trained on deep representations achieve high accuracy when evaluated on the same language but exhibit poor cross-lingual generalization. In contrast, probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages, despite achieving lower within-language performance. Together, these results suggest that LLMs first form a language-agnostic representation of problem difficulty, which subsequently becomes language-specific. This closely aligns with existing findings in LLM interpretability showing that models tend to operate in an abstract conceptual space before producing language-specific outputs. We demonstrate that this two-stage representational process extends beyond semantic content to high-level meta-cognitive properties such as problem-difficulty estimation.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
